description: Two Computer science student looking to create a fun fast project.
summary:
SPHEREx is mapping the entire sky in 102 near-infrared bands, and most of the known comets and brown dwarfs were found by volunteers doing the simplest thing possible: comparing two images of the same patch taken at different times, and noticing one point of light had moved. The barrier is access, not data.

SphereX Sky-Time makes that comparison a button. Enter any coordinate and the page blinks that patch through its real SPHEREx observation dates, with a timeline that puts coverage and measured brightness on one axis and leaves the gaps in the schedule visible. A second plate walks through all 102 wavelengths, with an on-the-fly spectrum and a false-colour composite. The five challenge targets open instantly; any other coordinate on the sky builds live from the NASA archive.

We built it so anyone can experience discovery rather than read about it — the moment of noticing something for yourself. Every frame in a sequence shares one brightness curve, so a change you see is a change in the sky.
details:
What it does 
SphereX Sky-Time shows one small patch of sky as it changes. You give a coordinate and it plays every date SPHEREx has observed that patch as a blink, so anything that moved between visits stands out at once. This is the comparison that found Pluto, and the one volunteers have used to find most known comets and brown dwarfs. A timeline below the image puts observing coverage and measured brightness on one axis, so the gaps in the schedule stay visible.

A second plate shows the same patch in all 102 SPHEREx wavelengths, with a scrubber through the bands, a spectrum of the target, and a colour image built from three of those bands. The five challenge targets open instantly, and any other coordinate on the sky is built live from the NASA archive.

How it works 
A Python pipeline queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive for every exposure of a position, subtracts the zodiacal background, reads the quality mask from the archive's own flag names, and propagates each target's proper motion to the exposure date (Barnard's Star moves 273.8 arcseconds between J2000 and 2026, so the catalogue position alone gives empty sky). It then reprojects all dates onto one grid and renders them through a single shared brightness curve. A FastAPI service on Cloud Run serves sequences, cubes, spectra and build progress, and a React and TypeScript frontend on Vercel draws both plates and applies colour palettes locally, so ten palettes cost no extra data. The URL carries the coordinate to five decimals, so any view is a link you can share or embed.

Impact The people
this is for are not researchers. Volunteers and students can look at the same patch twice, which is what actually produces discoveries, without learning FITS files or archive syntax. Teachers get a link to a specific piece of sky. Anyone curious gets the feeling of noticing something themselves, which is the point: we did not build a research tool, we built the shortest path to the ache of discovery.

Creativity and care 

The blink is the product, so every frame is decoded before play is enabled, because a flicker would read as a real change in the sky. Palettes are applied in the browser to planes that are already downloaded. If a star saturates, or a brown dwarf is too faint for a single exposure, the page says so instead of drawing something that looks like a detection. We also avoided fake variability from per-frame scaling, corrected positions for proper motion, kept archive failures distinct from empty results, and prebuilt the five targets so a visitor with poor Wi-Fi never waits.

Tools 

Python 3.14, NumPy, Astropy, reproject, photutils, Pillow, hpgeom, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Google Cloud Run, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Vercel, GitHub, with over 140 automated tests and one pull request per build phase.
